content: On February 1, 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern following a meeting of the International Health Regulations (IHR) Emergency Committee on Zika virus. This declaration was based on the clustering of cases of microcephaly, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and other neurological conditions in areas affected by Zika virus transmission. Since late 2015, northeastern Brazil has reported up to a 20-fold increase in congenital microcephaly cases. By August 18, 2016, 17 countries or territories had reported cases of microcephaly and/or other central nervous system malformations potentially linked to Zika virus infection or suggestive of congenital infection. Three of these countries reported microcephaly in neonates born to mothers who had traveled to Zika-affected areas but resided in countries without endemic Zika virus transmission. The purpose of this document is to provide guidance on the screening, clinical assessment, neuroimaging, and laboratory investigations of neonates and infants born to women residing in areas of Zika virus transmission. It updates the WHO interim guidance on the assessment of infants with microcephaly in the context of Zika virus, published on March 4, 2016. This update includes summaries of recent evidence supporting the recommendations and operational considerations for implementation. The guidance aims to inform the development of national and local clinical protocols and health policies related to neonatal and infant care in the context of Zika virus transmission. However, it does not serve as a comprehensive guide for managing Zika virus infections or neonatal neurological conditions, including microcephaly. Microcephaly is a condition where an infant's head circumference is smaller than expected for their age and sex. It is defined as a head circumference more than two standard deviations below the median for age and sex, with severe microcephaly being more than three standard deviations below the median. Head circumference reflects intracranial volume and is a critical measure for monitoring brain growth. Microcephaly can result from various genetic factors, such as chromosomal and metabolic disorders, as well as non-genetic causes, including congenital infections, teratogen exposure, perinatal brain injuries, and severe malnutrition. Microcephaly present at birth often indicates underlying brain pathology and is associated with neurological sequelae, including developmental delay, intellectual impairment, hearing and visual deficits, and epilepsy. Congenital Zika virus syndrome encompasses a range of manifestations beyond microcephaly, including craniofacial disproportion, spasticity, seizures, irritability, brainstem dysfunction (e.g., swallowing difficulties), limb contractures, hearing and ocular abnormalities, and brain anomalies detected via neuroimaging. Neuroimaging findings in affected neonates include cortical and subcortical calcifications, cortical malformations, simplified gyral patterns, brainstem and cerebellar hypoplasia, and ventriculomegaly. These abnormalities suggest a congenital syndrome attributable to in utero Zika virus infection, similar to congenital rubella or cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections. Evidence from observational, cohort, and case-control studies strongly supports the causal relationship between Zika virus and microcephaly, as well as other neurological complications constituting congenital Zika virus syndrome. Long-term clinical follow-up of infants born to women with confirmed Zika virus infection during pregnancy is necessary. As more evidence emerges, WHO will update the clinical profile associated with congenital Zika virus syndrome. Initial clinical and anthropometric assessment of neonates should include head circumference measurement within the first 24 hours of life. For term neonates, WHO Child Growth Standards should be used, while INTERGROWTH-21 standards are preferred if gestational age is accurately known. For preterm neonates, INTERGROWTH-21 standards for gestational age and sex should be applied. Mothers should be asked about clinical signs and symptoms of Zika virus infection during pregnancy, including laboratory confirmation and the timing of possible infection. Neonates should be examined for craniofacial disproportion, which may indicate poor brain growth. Microcephaly is associated with numerous genetic and non-genetic etiologies, including congenital infections such as TORCH infections (toxoplasmosis, rubella, CMV, herpes), syphilis, varicella-zoster, parvovirus B19, and HIV. Non-genetic causes also include teratogen exposure (e.g., alcohol, ionizing radiation), perinatal brain injuries (e.g., hypoxia-ischemia, trauma), and severe malnutrition. In the context of congenital infections, microcephaly often predicts worse neurodevelopmental outcomes. Studies have shown a correlation between the degree of microcephaly and the likelihood of neurological impairment. For example, children with head circumferences between -2 and -3 standard deviations have a lower risk of intellectual disability compared to those with head circumferences below -3 standard deviations. However, not all children with congenital Zika virus syndrome present with microcephaly, and some may have normal head circumferences at birth but exhibit craniofacial disproportion, suggesting relatively poor brain growth.
